patient.name: Baby Thompson
patient.chiefComplaint: Term newborn, meconium-stained fluid at delivery, floppy and not breathing

history.hpi: Just-delivered term male infant, approximately 39 weeks gestation by mother's dates. Amniotic fluid was thick and meconium-stained at rupture of membranes. Immediately after delivery of the body, the infant is floppy with poor tone, weak/absent respiratory effort, and no crying.
history.events: Delivered on scene by crew moments ago following an otherwise uncomplicated labor; meconium noted at rupture of membranes prompted immediate post-delivery assessment

scene.dispatch: Crew on scene for imminent delivery, newborn now delivered, requesting newborn assessment
scene.location: Single-family home, bedroom, mother on the bed, newborn on a prepared warming surface at bedside
scene.safety: No hazards to crew noted; second crew member available for two-person newborn care
scene.bystanders: Mother present, anxious, second EMS provider assisting with mother's ongoing care
visualCues: Newborn on warming surface, thick meconium staining visible on skin and umbilical cord
No audible cry, chest wall not moving with visible effort
Warming supplies and BVM with appropriately sized mask already staged

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: A term male newborn has just delivered through thick meconium-stained fluid and presents floppy with poor tone and absent respiratory effort, meeting criteria for immediate resuscitation rather than routine care.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Meconium staining visible around mouth and nose, no spontaneous airway clearing
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Absent respiratory effort, no chest rise
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Weak, slow pulse palpable at umbilical stump
clinicalPresentation.pupils: Not clinically assessed at this age
otherFindings: Thick meconium staining on skin and cord
Heart rate estimated at approximately 55 bpm on auscultation

transitions.condition: Crew immediately dries, warms, and stimulates the infant while positioning the airway in sniffing position and clearing meconium from the mouth and nose given signs of respiratory distress with airway obstruction.
Crew delays initiating the dry-warm-stimulate and airway-clearing sequence, allowing ongoing apnea and bradycardia.

phases.name: Dried, warmed, positioned, airway cleared
phases.description: Crew dries and warms the infant, positions the airway in the sniffing position, and suctions the mouth then nose given visible meconium and signs of airway obstruction. The infant remains apneic with a heart rate below 100.
phases.triggerCondition: Given the floppy tone, absent respiratory effort, and visible meconium, the crew proceeds directly to warming, airway positioning, and targeted suctioning rather than routine skin-to-skin care.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Cleared of visible meconium after suctioning mouth then nose
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Still absent respiratory effort after stimulation
clinicalPresentation.pupils: Not clinically assessed at this age
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Poor tone, minimal response to stimulation
otherFindings: Infant dried and wrapped, head covered where possible
Airway suctioned mouth then nose, meconium cleared
No spontaneous respiratory effort despite stimulation
Heart rate approximately 58 bpm on reassessment

expectedActions.shortAction: Dry, warm, and stimulate infant; wrap in dry towel, cover head
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Wrap infant in dry towel or thermal blanket to keep infant as warm as possible during resuscitation; keep head covered if possible
expectedActions.rationale: Hypothermia worsens outcomes in a compromised newborn and stimulation may itself trigger respiratory effort.

expectedActions.shortAction: Position airway in sniffing position; suction mouth then nose given visible meconium
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If weak cry, signs of respiratory distress, poor tone, or preterm gestation then position airway (sniffing position) and clear airway as needed. If signs of respiratory distress with airway obstruction, suction mouth then nose; routine suctioning is not recommended
expectedActions.rationale: Meconium with airway obstruction and poor tone meets the protocol's criteria for targeted suctioning, unlike a vigorous newborn.

expectedActions.shortAction: Apply cardiac monitor and pulse oximetry to guide resuscitation
expectedActions.rationale: Heart rate trend is the primary indicator of resuscitation effectiveness going forward.

transitions.condition: Despite warming, positioning, and airway clearing, the infant remains apneic with a heart rate below 100 bpm, meeting criteria for positive pressure ventilation.

phases.name: PPV initiated for HR under 100
phases.description: Crew initiates BVM positive pressure ventilation at 40-60 breaths per minute with room air, reassessing heart rate every 30 seconds. Heart rate improves toward normal with effective ventilation.
phases.triggerCondition: With heart rate persistently below 100 bpm and no spontaneous respiratory effort, the crew begins positive pressure ventilation per the Evaluate step of the resuscitation sequence.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent with BVM ventilation, good chest rise
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Assisted via BVM at 40-60/min, chest rise present with each breath
clinicalPresentation.pupils: Not clinically assessed at this age
otherFindings: Heart rate improving with each 30-second reassessment
Chest rise adequate with squeeze-release technique
SpO2 trending upward toward age-appropriate target

expectedActions.shortAction: Initiate BVM ventilation with room air at 40-60 breaths/min for 90 seconds
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Initiate BVM ventilation with room air at 40–60 breaths per minute for 90 seconds with room air
expectedActions.rationale: Effective PPV is the single most important intervention for a newborn with bradycardia and apnea.

expectedActions.shortAction: Evaluate heart rate every 30 seconds during ventilation
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Primary indicator of effective ventilation is improvement in heart rate. Evaluate heart rate every 30 seconds
expectedActions.rationale: Heart rate response determines whether to continue current management or escalate to compressions/epinephrine.

expectedActions.shortAction: Use minimum rate/volume needed for chest rise and HR change (squeeze-release technique)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Rates and volumes of ventilation required can be variable, only use the minimum necessary rate and volume to achieve chest rise and a change in heart rate; can control rate and volume by saying "squeeze, release"
expectedActions.rationale: Excessive volume/pressure risks pneumothorax in the newborn lung.

phases.name: Resuscitation sequence delayed
phases.description: Crew delays the dry-warm-stimulate and airway-clearing sequence, allowing the infant to remain apneic and bradycardic without intervention.
phases.triggerCondition: Distracted by maternal care or uncertain how to proceed with a meconium-stained, floppy newborn, the crew delays initiating the resuscitation sequence.

clinicalPresentation.pupils: Not clinically assessed at this age
otherFindings: No drying, warming, or airway clearing yet performed
Heart rate trending downward on reassessment
Ongoing heat loss from wet skin

expectedActions.shortAction: Immediately begin dry-warm-stimulate, position airway, and suction mouth then nose
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Most newborns require only drying, warming, and stimulating to help them transition from fetal respiration to newborn respiration. The resuscitation sequence can be remembered as Dry, Warm, and Stimulate – Ventilate – Evaluate – and Resuscitate
expectedActions.rationale: Ongoing delay compounds hypothermia and worsening bradycardia; the resuscitation sequence must begin without further delay.
